name: Gaul
title: Social Hierarchy of Ancient Gaul: From Kings to the Enslaved
period: c. 121–52 BCE (free Gaul in the time of Julius Caesar)

tiers.name: Kings and chief magistrates
tiers.you: You have been chosen vergobret of the Aedui for a year: your power is much like a king’s, but the council’s rules bind you.
tiers.kid: Each Gallic tribe had a council of elders and a leader, at first a king and later often a leader chosen every year.
tiers.rise: In many tribes the rule of kings gave way to magistrates elected for a year, whose powers the council of elders limited. In a time of crisis the tribes could unite under a single war leader, as they did under Vercingetorix, though even then the factions remained.
tiers.why: The tribe, made up of one or more smaller units the Romans called pagi, was the basic unit of Gallic politics.

tiers.name: Druids
tiers.you: You perform the sacrifices of your people and judge their disputes over crimes, inheritances and boundaries, and you pay no taxes and do no military service.
tiers.kid: Druids were priests and teachers who learned everything by heart, settled quarrels and led the ceremonies for the gods.
tiers.rise: Pupils might stay in training for up to twenty years, learning a great body of verse by heart, since the druids held it unlawful to write their teaching down. Caesar says their teaching came from Britain, and that Gauls who wished to study it closely went there.
tiers.why: The druids were the learned class: priests, judges, teachers and keepers of religious and legal tradition.

tiers.name: Warrior nobles
tiers.you: You ride to war at the head of your followers, a torc at your neck and your moustache grown over your mouth; your standing rests on war and on the men who look to you as their patron.
tiers.kid: Noble warriors rode horses into battle and wore metal neck rings called torcs, some of them made of gold.
tiers.rise: The sources say little of how a man entered the nobility. After the conquest the Gaulish upper class took up Roman ways quickly, and Gauls served Rome as horsemen.
tiers.why: The second honoured class, in Caesar’s account, was the equites, the “horsemen”: a warrior aristocracy.

tiers.name: Smiths and craftsmen
tiers.you: You work bronze and gold, hammering spirals and S-scrolls into a noble’s torc or helmet, and Roman merchants come to buy your weapons and jewellery.
tiers.kid: Gallic smiths made beautiful things from gold and bronze, decorated with swirling patterns.
tiers.rise: The sources do not say how a smith learned his craft or whether it passed from father to son. As Rome’s demand for gold grew, gold production in the Celtic lands rose sharply.

tiers.name: The free people
tiers.you: You are one of the free people of your tribe; the druids keep the calendar that tells you when the seasons and festivals come, and when war comes you take refuge behind the ramparts of a hill fort.
tiers.kid: Most Gauls were ordinary free people who wore warm trousers and worshipped many gods of nature.
tiers.rise: The sources record no path upward for ordinary Gauls. A free person could fall into slavery for debt or as a punishment, and the Romans enslaved about a million Gauls in the Gallic Wars.
tiers.why: Of the free Gauls who were neither nobles nor druids, the great majority, the ancient writers say least.

tiers.name: Enslaved people
tiers.you: You were taken in a raid on a neighbouring tribe and now belong to another; your children will be born slaves unless your owner sets you free.
tiers.kid: Some people in Gaul were enslaved, often after being captured in war, and their children were enslaved too.
tiers.rise: Freedom came only by manumission, which was possible but is not described; a slave’s children were born into slavery.
tiers.why: Slavery among the Celts was very likely much like that of Greece and Rome.
